note: Quick questions of the Cyber box. They are practice only: they never enter the decision ledger or the knowledge score. The first option is the right one; the game shuffles the order.

questions.qAr: A message says: "You won a prize! Tap the link now." What do you do?
options: I don't tap and I tell a parent
I tap fast before it ends
I send it to all my friends
questions.whyAr: Surprise prize messages are a common trap to steal data.

questions.qAr: What do you check first in a message from a stranger?
questions.whyAr: The sender's address exposes many fake messages.

questions.qAr: A message says: "Your account will close in a minute!" This rush is…
options: A trick sign, so I pause and check
A reason to send my password now
questions.whyAr: Scammers rush you so you don't think.

questions.qAr: A friend sends a strange link with no words. What do you do?
options: I ask another way if they really sent it
I open it; my friend sent it
I forward it to the group
questions.whyAr: Your friend's account may be hacked.

questions.qAr: Where do you type your login?
options: On the official site I open myself
On any link I get in a message
In a window that pops up
questions.whyAr: Open the official site yourself. Don't follow message links.

questions.qAr: What is a fake message that tries to steal your data called?
questions.whyAr: A phishing message uses a name you trust to take your data.

questions.qAr: A "bank" message has mistakes and asks for your PIN. What is it?
questions.whyAr: A bank never asks for your PIN in a message.

questions.qAr: A short link hides where it goes. What do you do?
options: I check its source before I open it
I open it to find out
I send it to a friend to try
questions.whyAr: An unknown link may take you to a fake page.

questions.qAr: What is a computer "virus"?
options: Bad program that sticks to files and spreads
questions.whyAr: A virus spreads when you open an infected file.

questions.qAr: A message says send it to 10 friends to win. What do you do?
options: I ignore it and don't send it
I send it to 20 to win more
questions.whyAr: Chain messages spread bad links between friends.

questions.qAr: Which password is strongest?
options: A long phrase with letters, numbers, symbols
questions.whyAr: Length and variety make guessing hard.

questions.qAr: A caller asks for the verification code you got. What do you do?
options: I never give it to anyone
I give it if told he's staff
I send it in a message
questions.whyAr: The code is yours alone. No official service asks for it.

questions.qAr: Do you use the same password for all accounts?
options: No, each account has its own
Yes, so it's easy to remember
questions.whyAr: If one leaks, the other accounts stay safe.

questions.qAr: Why use two-step verification?
options: Guards the account even if the password is known
questions.whyAr: The second step is an extra wall against hackers.

questions.qAr: A friend wants your account password to play. What do you do?
options: I say sorry and don't share
I give it; he's my friend
I send it to him in the group
questions.whyAr: A password is a secret, not shared even with friends.

questions.qAr: Where do you keep your many passwords safe?
options: On a paper on the desk
In a message to my friend
questions.whyAr: A password manager keeps them encrypted behind one lock.

questions.qAr: Which one makes a bad password?
questions.whyAr: Many know your birth date, and it's easy to guess.

questions.qAr: You hear your password leaked. What do you do?
options: I change it now wherever I used it
questions.whyAr: Hackers try a leaked password on your other accounts.

questions.qAr: What is "ransomware"?
options: It locks your files and asks for money
questions.whyAr: A backup is the best protection from it.

questions.qAr: When to change your password?
options: When I think someone knows it
When a friend asks me to
questions.whyAr: Any doubt it leaked is enough to change it.

questions.qAr: Where do you download games and apps?
options: From any link in an ad
From a file a stranger sent
questions.whyAr: Official stores check apps before publishing them.

questions.qAr: A simple colour game asks to see your messages. What do you do?
options: I refuse; it doesn't need it
I agree, then forget about it
questions.whyAr: Give an app only what it needs to work.

questions.qAr: A pop-up: "Your device is infected! Get this program." What do you do?
options: I type my details in it
questions.whyAr: These scare pop-ups spread bad programs.

questions.qAr: What do you check before getting a new app?
questions.whyAr: These details reveal copycat apps.

questions.qAr: A "free hacked" copy of a paid game…
options: May carry bad programs, so I avoid it
A good deal, so I download it
questions.whyAr: Pirated programs are a common door for viruses.

questions.qAr: What is a "Trojan horse" program?
options: A useful-looking program that hides harm
questions.whyAr: So we only download from official stores.

questions.qAr: A torch app asks to read your messages. It is…
questions.whyAr: A torch shines without your messages.

questions.qAr: What is a computer "worm"?
options: Bad program that moves alone between devices
questions.whyAr: A worm spreads without you tapping anything. Updates stop it.

questions.qAr: A game has one star and comments warn against it. What do you do?
options: I download it and ignore comments
questions.whyAr: People's ratings reveal bad apps.

questions.qAr: What is "spyware"?
options: It secretly watches you and steals your info
questions.whyAr: It often comes with apps from outside the store.

questions.qAr: An official system update pops up. What do you do?
options: I update as soon as I can
questions.whyAr: Updates close security holes that hackers use.

questions.qAr: What is a backup good for?
options: I restore my files if lost or the device breaks
questions.whyAr: A backup rescues your photos and files.

questions.qAr: Where do safe updates come from?
options: From device settings or the official store
From a link in a message
questions.whyAr: A fake update may be a bad program.

questions.qAr: Where do you keep a backup of your important files?
options: Somewhere else, not on the device
questions.whyAr: If the device breaks, the copy stays somewhere safe.

questions.qAr: How often do you make a backup?
questions.whyAr: Regular backups save your newest files.

questions.qAr: Why do companies release security updates?
options: To close holes that are found
questions.whyAr: A security hole is an open door for a hacker.

questions.qAr: What is a "security hole"?
options: A program mistake that lets a hacker in
questions.whyAr: Updates are what close the holes.

questions.qAr: Where is it best to turn on auto-update?
options: In both the system and the apps
questions.whyAr: Auto-update protects you even if you forget.

questions.qAr: Ransomware hits your device. You have a backup. What is the fix?
options: I restore my files from backup
I download a tool the hacker sent
questions.whyAr: Paying promises nothing. The backup restores the files.

questions.qAr: How do you make sure your backup works?
options: I test it by restoring a file
I delete the original and see
questions.whyAr: An untested backup may fail when you need it.

questions.qAr: A public Wi-Fi with no password. What do you avoid on it?
questions.whyAr: Other people may watch open networks.

questions.qAr: A stranger in a game asks for your home address. What do you do?
options: I don't tell him; I tell a parent
I tell him because he is nice
I send him a photo of my home
questions.whyAr: Personal information is not for strangers.

questions.qAr: You see something scary or upsetting online. What do you do?
options: I tell an adult I trust
I share it with my friends
questions.whyAr: Trusted adults help you do the right thing.

questions.qAr: Before you leave a shared device, what do you do?
options: I sign out of my accounts
I write the password on paper beside it
questions.whyAr: Signing out keeps others out of your account.

questions.qAr: Which phone screen lock is best?
options: A code or fingerprint only I know
No lock, so it is faster
questions.whyAr: A screen lock protects what's on a lost phone.

questions.qAr: What is a "firewall"?
options: A guard that blocks connections not allowed
A real wall around a computer
questions.whyAr: It watches what goes in and out of your device on the network.

questions.qAr: What does "antivirus" do?
options: Scans the device and removes bad programs
questions.whyAr: It needs constant updates to know new threats.

questions.qAr: What is a "botnet"?
options: Infected devices a hacker controls remotely
questions.whyAr: Your unprotected device may join them without you knowing.

questions.qAr: A game friend asks for your photo and school name. What do you do?
options: I refuse and tell my parents
I send them; we play together
I send only the school name
questions.whyAr: A game-only friend is still a stranger.

questions.qAr: What is a "logic bomb"?
options: Bad code that waits for a set time to run
questions.whyAr: It sleeps inside a program until its time comes.
